screens.title: GPIO Configuration and Digital I/O
screens.subtitle: How the TM4C123G connects software to pins, and the register steps to read and write digital signals

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn how general purpose input and output works on the TM4C123G and why the register sequence matters. GPIO is the basic bridge between your program and the real world: a pin can be an input that reads a button or a sensor, or an output that drives an LED or a motor. You will see how the microcontroller exposes ports through memory-mapped registers, why the clock gate must be enabled before anything else, and how direction, digital enable, and data registers work together to safely change pin state. We'll use Port F and the blue LED on pin two as a running example so you can follow a direct, reproducible workflow. Practically, this means you will be able to enable a port, configure pins, and blink LEDs or sample switches. Along the way we will call out a common mistake — forgetting the clock enable — and how the symptom looks in hardware. By the end you should understand the four-register pattern and be ready to adapt it to other ports. Consider what you would measure on a pin when you flip it high or low; that question will guide the hands-on steps.

keyIdea.title: Core idea
keyIdea.text: Enable the port clock, set pin direction, enable digital function, then read/write the data register.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › GPIO Configuration and Digital I/O
GPIO Configuration and Digital I/O
Practical register steps to read switches and drive LEDs on the TM4C123G.

GPIO is the most direct way your program interacts with hardware pins. The TM4C123G exposes each port through memory-mapped registers, so software reads and writes normal addresses to change electrical signals.

We will follow a repeatable four-step pattern: enable the GPIO clock, set the pin direction, enable the pin's digital function, then read or write the data register. That pattern lets you control LEDs and read switches safely and predictably.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you will be able to do after this lesson

narration.text: These learning objectives describe the concrete skills you will practice. First, you will be able to explain how GPIO ports work on the TM4C123G, using the specific terms 'port', 'pin', and 'memory-mapped register.' This matters because precise vocabulary helps you find the right addresses and bits. Second, you will enable the clock for a GPIO port and configure pins as inputs or outputs; that step is essential because registers are inaccessible until the clock is active. Third, you will read and write the data register to observe voltage changes and sample inputs, a practical skill for testing hardware. Fourth, you will understand the role of the direction register, the digital enable register, and the alternate function register when pins are shared with peripherals. Each objective includes a short reason why it matters and a small mnemonic to help you remember the register order. Treat these as verification milestones: once you can blink PF2 and configure PF0 as input, you meet the competency for basic digital input and output.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Applied Practice
screens.subtitle: How to verify the objectives in hardware and code

narration.text: This second objectives screen focuses on practical verification and why each step matters when you run the code on a LaunchPad. First, explaining how GPIO works means you can locate the correct base addresses for ports and avoid affecting unrelated pins. For example, understanding that Port F bit two maps to PF2 helps you target the blue LED without touching PF0. Second, enabling the clock is not optional: without SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO you read back zeros and writes have no effect. Third, using the data register correctly means choosing between a full write and masked writes; masked writes protect other pins on the same port. Fourth, recognizing alternate functions prevents accidental conflicts when a pin is shared with UART or PWM. Each objective includes a practical milestone: blink PF2, configure PF0 as input, and measure voltages with a multimeter. These verification steps confirm both conceptual understanding and hands-on competence.

screens.title: What is GPIO?
screens.subtitle: Definition, practical examples, and why it matters

narration.text: GPIO stands for General Purpose Input/Output. At its core GPIO is a programmable electrical pin that your software can either read from or drive. As an input, a pin senses external signals like a button press or a sensor output. As an output, the pin sources or sinks current to light an LED, toggle a transistor, or command a motor driver. On the TM4C123G, ports are grouped into named banks A through F and each port exposes registers at fixed memory addresses — that is memory-mapped input and output. This design means normal load and store instructions access hardware registers. A concrete example is PF2 on a LaunchPad: when you write the correct bit in the port's data register, the blue LED turns on and you can measure the voltage with a multimeter. A common misconception is to assume the pin will work before enabling its clock: on this MCU you must enable the clock gating bit for a port — otherwise reads and writes behave as if the peripheral is powered down. Key takeaway: GPIO gives your code direct control of physical signals, but that control is mediated by a small set of registers and correct sequencing.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: GPIO are programmable pins accessed via memory-mapped registers for simple digital I/O.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › What is GPIO?
Definition
GPIO are pins you configure as inputs or outputs. Inputs read a physical signal; outputs drive one.
Input example
Read a switch to detect button presses and trigger software events.
Output example
Drive an LED to indicate status, toggling the pin high and low in a loop.
Misconception
Assuming a pin is usable before enabling its port clock. The TM4C123G requires the RCGCGPIO bit to be set first.
Key Takeaway

GPIO maps software writes and reads to physical voltages; sequencing matters to avoid inert peripherals.

Concrete example — PF2 LED
// PF2 is the blue LED
#define PF2 (1<<2)
// After enabling clock and DEN, write GPIODATA |= PF2 to turn on LED
// Clear bit to turn it off
Measure the pin voltage when set high to confirm the LED is driven. Use the example blink code later to see this in action.
Check your understanding
How would you confirm a pin is configured as input? Answer: read the GPIODIR bit for that pin and then sample GPIODATA while toggling the external signal.

screens.title: Ports A–F and Pin Mapping
screens.subtitle: How ports and pins are organized on the TM4C123G

narration.text: The TM4C123G organizes GPIO into labeled ports: A, B, C, D, E, and F. Each port can have up to eight pins, numbered zero through seven, and some physical pins on the package double as special peripheral functions. In practical terms this means the microcontroller provides a small set of base addresses, one per port, and within each port the registers control up to eight bits. For example, Port F includes PF0 through PF4 on many LaunchPad boards; PF2 is commonly the blue LED. A useful mental model is a two-level hierarchy: the port is the container with its own base address and control registers, and pins are individual bits inside those registers. The hierarchy helps you avoid mistakes like writing to the wrong port base address. A common pitfall is assuming every port has eight usable pins; some package pins are reserved for functions like debugging, so the practical pin count for GPIO operations can be lower. Remember to consult the device pin map when targeting a specific physical pin. The key practical outcome is that your code addresses the port base and manipulates bit positions corresponding to pins.

keyIdea.title: Ports hierarchy
keyIdea.text: Ports are containers (A–F); pins are bits within a port's registers. Map names like PF2 to bit positions.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Ports A–F and Pin Mapping
Ports and pins
Each port (A–F) has a base address and up to eight pins. Pins are addressed as bits within the port registers.
Port as container
One base address with multiple registers like DIR, DEN, DATA for all pins of that port.
Pin as bit
Pin number maps to a bit position: PF2 is bit two in Port F's registers.
Practical note
Some package pins are used for debugging or alternate functions, so count usable GPIO pins carefully for your board.
Visual mapping
P0
P1
P2
P3
P4
For Port F on the LaunchPad, PF2 controls the blue LED. Code uses a bit mask such as one shifted left by two to change PF2 without disturbing other bits.
Why it matters

Understanding the port/pin hierarchy reduces address errors and prevents unintentional changes to unrelated pins on the same port.

screens.title: Memory-Mapped I/O and Registers
screens.subtitle: How the TM4C123G represents GPIO in memory

narration.text: The TM4C123G uses a memory-mapped input and output model: registers that control GPIO appear at specific memory addresses and your code reads and writes them like variables. For Port F the RCGCGPIO register at 0x400FE608 controls port clocks; GPIODIR at 0x40025400 sets pin directions; GPIODEN at 0x4002551C enables digital function; and GPIODATA at 0x400253FC reads and writes pin states. Each register occupies a fixed address, and writing specific bits in those registers toggles behavior for the corresponding pins. A critical practical point is the sequence: enabling the peripheral clock first, then configuring direction and digital enable, and only afterward accessing data. If you try to set bits before the clock is on, writes will have no effect and reads will not reflect the expected state. Think of registers as mapped control panels: the addresses are panel locations, and each bit is a labeled switch. When moving from code to hardware, you must also be mindful of bitwise operations to avoid overwriting neighboring pin settings. This register architecture is what makes the simple PF2 blink example possible and predictable. Memory-Mapped I/O and Registers means gpio registers are normal memory addresses; write and read them to control pins, observing required sequencing.. In practical terms, how the tm4c123g represents gpio in memory. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Memory-mapped model
keyIdea.text: GPIO registers are normal memory addresses; write and read them to control pins, observing required sequencing.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Memory-Mapped I/O and Registers
Key GPIO registers (Port F addresses)
  • SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO (0x400FE608) — enables port clocks; set bit 5 for Port F.
  • GPIO_PORTF_DIR_R (0x40025400) — direction: 0=input, 1=output per bit.
  • GPIO_PORTF_DEN_R (0x4002551C) — digital enable for pins used as digital I/O.
  • GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R (0x400253FC) — read inputs and write outputs; mask-based addressing exists.
Register values are manipulated with bitwise operations. Use OR to set bits and AND with complement to clear bits so that you don't accidentally change other pins on the same port.
Sequence reminder
Enable clock → wait for it to stabilize → configure direction → enable digital function → access data.
Common mistake

Skipping the clock enable results in code that appears to run but has no effect on pins. The symptom is that LEDs won't change state even though your code sets the bits.

Check your understanding
Why must you wait after setting the RCGCGPIO bit? Because the peripheral clock needs time to stabilize before registers respond predictably.

screens.title: Enable the GPIO Clock (RCGCGPIO)
screens.subtitle: Why clock gating matters and how to verify it

narration.text: The first register you touch is the Run-Mode Clock Gating Control for GPIO, commonly named RCGCGPIO at address 0x400FE608. This register contains one bit per port; to enable Port F you set bit five, which corresponds to a value of 0x20. Enabling the clock powers the port's registers so subsequent writes and reads are effective. A practical pattern is to set the bit and then poll the same bit until it reads back as set, which indicates stability. If you skip this step your writes to GPIODIR or GPIODEN will have no visible effect — the hardware simply ignores them. A concrete verification method is to set the clock bit, then try to set a direction bit and read it back; if it remains zero the clock did not enable. Remember that clock gating is a common energy-saving feature on modern MCUs; it's deliberate and required. When debugging, always check SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO before spending time on higher-level code. This step prevents wasted debugging time and is the single most frequent cause of non-responsive GPIO during initial bring-up. Enable the GPIO Clock (RCGCGPIO) means set sysctl_rcgcgpio bit for the port first and wait for it to stabilize before configuring pins.. In practical terms, why clock gating matters and how to verify it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Clock gating
keyIdea.text: Set SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO bit for the port first and wait for it to stabilize before configuring pins.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Enable the GPIO Clock (RCGCGPIO)
RCGCGPIO — the first step
Set bit 5 (0x20) to enable Port F's clock at address 0x400FE608.
Verification
  • Write SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO |= 0x20;
  • Poll until (SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO & 0x20) is nonzero.
  • Then configure GPIODIR and GPIODEN.
Debug tip
If LEDs don't respond, check that the clock bit is set and reads back as set. If not, power sequencing or incorrect address usage might be the cause.
Symptom

Writes to direction and data registers appear to do nothing. Often caused by missing or wrong RCGCGPIO enable.

screens.title: Direction and Digital Enable Registers
screens.subtitle: GPIODIR and GPIODEN: making pins inputs or outputs and enabling digital function

narration.text: Two registers control the basic behavior of pins: GPIODIR and GPIODEN. The direction register, GPIODIR, sets each pin as input when a bit is zero and as output when a bit is one. The digital enable register, GPIODEN, activates the digital function for pins that will be used for digital input and output. Both must be set appropriately for a pin to behave as expected. For example, to make PF2 an output you set bit two in GPIODIR and also set the same bit in GPIODEN so the pin is enabled for digital operation. A common oversight is configuring direction but forgetting to set DEN; the pin may not drive a visible voltage without DEN enabled. The order is flexible after the clock is up, but both settings must be present before attempting data transfers. Practically you will use OR to set bits and AND with complement to clear them, which preserves other pins' configurations. This approach ensures that changing one pin does not unintentionally modify neighboring pins on the same port. Direction and Digital Enable Registers means set gpiodir bits to choose input/output; set gpioden to enable pins for digital i/o.. In practical terms, gpiodir and gpioden: making pins inputs or outputs and enabling digital function. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: DIR and DEN
keyIdea.text: Set GPIODIR bits to choose input/output; set GPIODEN to enable pins for digital I/O.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Direction and Digital Enable Registers
GPIODIR — set direction
0 = input, 1 = output per bit. Use OR to set and AND with complement to clear bits.
Example
To make PF2 an output: GPIO_PORTF_DIR_R |= (1 << 2); To make PF0 an input: GPIO_PORTF_DIR_R &= ~(1 << 0);
GPIODEN — enable digital
Set DEN bit for each pin used for digital I/O. A pin without DEN will not act as a digital input or output.
Practical note

Always enable DEN for pins used digitally; otherwise reads and writes may be ignored or the pin remains tri-stated.

Key Takeaway

Both direction and digital enable must be configured for a pin to operate as a reliable digital I/O.

screens.title: GPIODATA and Address Masking
screens.subtitle: How to read and write pin states and use address masks safely

narration.text: GPIODATA is the register used to read inputs and write outputs. On the TM4C123G the data register has a special address decoding: address bits nine through two act as a mask that selects which bits are affected by a write. Writing to the full base address 0x400253FC (mask 0xFF) affects all bits, while writing to an address that encodes a smaller mask affects only specific bits. This is a hardware convenience, but the simplest and most portable approach is to use the full data register address and use bitwise operations in software to change just the bits you want. For example, to set PF2 you can write GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R |= PF2 where PF2 is a one shifted left by two. To clear it use &= ~PF2. A common misconception is to perform plain assignments to GPIODATA without masking, which overwrites other pins on the same port. Always prefer read-modify-write with OR and AND unless you intentionally want to change every bit. In short, GPIODATA is the read/write view; use masking to protect unrelated pins or the address-mask feature when you need atomic bit updates.

keyIdea.title: Data register
keyIdea.text: Use read-modify-write on GPIODATA and understand the address mask behavior; avoid unintentional overwrites.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › GPIODATA and Address Masking
GPIODATA usage
Read inputs or write outputs. Prefer OR to set bits and AND with complement to clear bits.
Example operations
  • Set PF2: GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R |= (1 << 2);
  • Clear PF2: GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R &= ~(1 << 2);
  • Read PF2: value = GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R & (1 << 2);
Address mask note
Writes to different offsets within GPIODATA can affect only the bits selected by address bits [9:2]. This is a hardware mask that can be useful for atomic updates.
Practical advice

Unless you need the address-mask atomicity, use full GPIODATA and software masking for clarity and portability.

Key Takeaway

Protect other pins by using read-modify-write patterns on GPIODATA or by choosing masked addresses deliberately.

screens.title: Blink PF2 — Setup Code Explained
screens.subtitle: Step through the initialization sequence from the example

narration.text: Let's walk through the setup portion of the provided C example that blinks PF2. The code defines volatile pointers to the relevant addresses for SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO, GPIO_PORTF_DIR_R, GPIO_PORTF_DEN_R, and GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R. After these defines, the code enables the clock for Port F by OR-ing 0x20 into SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO_R and then loops while that bit remains zero until the clock is stable. Next it sets PF2 as an output by OR-ing PF2 into GPIO_PORTF_DIR_R and enables the digital function for PF2 by OR-ing into GPIO_PORTF_DEN_R. These three steps — clock enable, direction, and digital enable — prepare the hardware so the program can safely write to the data register. A common mistake is to forget the second read loop that waits for the clock; without it early writes may be ignored. The code keeps delay as a simple busy-loop and then uses bitwise set and clear operations on the data register to blink the LED. Understanding this initialization makes it straightforward to extend the code for multiple pins such as PF1, PF2 and PF3. Blink PF2 — Setup Code Explained means defines, enable clock, wait for stability, set direction, enable digital function — then you can write data.. In practical terms, step through the initialization sequence from the example. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Setup steps
keyIdea.text: Defines, enable clock, wait for stability, set direction, enable digital function — then you can write data.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Blink PF2 — Setup Code Explained
Setup code (excerpt)
#define SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO_R   (*((volatile uint32_t *)0x400FE608))
#define GPIO_PORTF_DIR_R    (*((volatile uint32_t *)0x40025400))
#define GPIO_PORTF_DEN_R    (*((volatile uint32_t *)0x4002551C))
#define GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R   (*((volatile uint32_t *)0x400253FC))

#define PF2 (1 << 2)

// Enable clock for GPIO Port F
SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO_R |= 0x20;
// Wait for clock to stabilize
while ((SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO_R & 0x20) == 0) {}

// Set PF2 as output
GPIO_PORTF_DIR_R |= PF2;
// Enable digital function for PF2
GPIO_PORTF_DEN_R |= PF2;
These lines define the registers and then perform the required initializations. The volatile pointer defines ensure direct memory access to the registers without compiler optimization removing reads or writes.
Why volatile?
Volatile prevents the compiler from optimizing away register reads/writes, ensuring each access reaches hardware.
Misconception

Assuming the compiler will keep register accesses without volatile may lead to missing writes or optimized-out loops.

Key Takeaway

Initialization is short but essential: no clock, no registers; no DEN, no digital behavior; no DIR, wrong direction.

screens.title: Blink PF2 — Main Loop and Bit Operations
screens.subtitle: How the loop toggles the LED and why masking matters

narration.text: Now examine the code's main loop: it repeatedly sets the PF2 bit in GPIODATA, calls a delay, clears the bit, and delays again. The key operations are GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R |= PF2 to set the bit and GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R &= ~PF2 to clear it. Using OR and AND with complement protects other pins on Port F; this read-modify-write pattern keeps unrelated outputs unchanged. The provided delay function is a busy loop — adequate for simple demonstrations but not precise. A common misconception is thinking equals assignment on GPIODATA will only change the target bit; using = instead of |= overwrites the entire register and can inadvertently change other pins. If you want multiple LEDs such as PF1, PF2, and PF3, compose the mask PF1|PF2|PF3 and apply the same OR/AND patterns. Practically, this loop demonstrates the full control flow: hardware initialized, then application logic toggles outputs by manipulating GPIODATA. As a reflective question, consider how you would change the code to create a repeating color pattern across three LEDs while preserving other pins. Blink PF2 — Main Loop and Bit Operations means use or to set bits, and with complement to clear them; avoid direct assignment to gpiodata unless you intend to overwrite all pins.. In practical terms, how the loop toggles the led and why masking matters. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Loop & masks
keyIdea.text: Use OR to set bits, AND with complement to clear them; avoid direct assignment to GPIODATA unless you intend to overwrite all pins.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Blink PF2 — Main Loop and Bit Operations
Main loop (excerpt)
while (1) {
    GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R |= PF2;   // Blue LED on
    delay(1000000);
    GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R &= ~PF2;  // Blue LED off
    delay(1000000);
}
This uses bitwise operations to change only PF2. Replace PF2 with a combined mask to toggle multiple LEDs together.
Common mistake
Using assignment like GPIO_PORTF_DATA_R = PF2 overwrites other pins and may disable unrelated outputs.
Pro Tip

When updating multiple pins, build a mask of all target bits and apply OR/AND to change them atomically in software.

screens.title: GPIO vs Alternate Functions
screens.subtitle: When to leave pins as GPIO and when to use AFSEL for peripherals

narration.text: Some pins on the TM4C123G are multiplexed with peripheral functions like UART, I2C, or PWM. The GPIO Alternate Function Select register, AFSEL, controls whether a pin is used for its alternate peripheral function or kept as general purpose. For basic digital input and output you typically leave AFSEL cleared so the pin behaves as GPIO; for peripherals you set AFSEL and configure the peripheral module instead. A practical contrast: use GPIO for simple LED or button control; use AFSEL when you need serial communication or PWM motor control on that pin. A common confusion is enabling both AFSEL and DEN simultaneously for the same pin; check the device data to see whether the peripheral requires clearing or setting DEN in coordination with AFSEL. In summary, choose GPIO for direct digital control and AFSEL when you need peripheral features. When starting a project, reserve pins you need for peripherals early to avoid conflicts with simple input and output code later. GPIO vs Alternate Functions means keep afsel cleared for gpio; set it to enable a pin's alternate peripheral function when required.. In practical terms, when to leave pins as gpio and when to use afsel for peripherals. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: AFSEL
keyIdea.text: Keep AFSEL cleared for GPIO; set it to enable a pin's alternate peripheral function when required.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › GPIO vs Alternate Functions
GPIO (direct control)
Best for simple on/off signals like LEDs and buttons. Keep AFSEL cleared and use DIR, DEN, and DATA registers.
When to use
Direct toggling, debounced button reads, status indicators, or simple logic-level outputs.
Alternate function (AFSEL)
Enable AFSEL when a pin must serve UART, I2C, PWM, or other peripheral roles. Then configure the peripheral module registers.
Important
Reserve pins for peripheral use early to avoid conflict with GPIO code that assumes control of those pins.
Check your understanding

If a pin needs to act as UART transmit, which register do you set? Answer: AFSEL and configure the UART peripheral, not just DEN and DIR for GPIO.

screens.title: Hands-on: Multi-LED Pattern on Port F
screens.subtitle: Configure PF1, PF2, PF3 as outputs and create a repeating color pattern

narration.text: For the hands-on activity you will configure Port F pins one, two, and three — the red, blue, and green LEDs — as outputs and implement a repeating pattern: red on for one second, blue on for one second, green on one second, then all three on for one second. The code follows the same sequence: enable the port clock, wait for stability, set the direction bits for PF1, PF2, PF3, enable DEN for those pins, and then toggle the GPIODATA bits with appropriate delays. Use masks such as (1<<1), (1<<2), and (1<<3), and combine them using bitwise OR when you want multiple LEDs on. After uploading the program, use a multimeter to measure pin voltage when each LED is HIGH and LOW to confirm expected behavior. This exercise reinforces register sequencing, masking, and timing. A common improvement is to replace the busy-wait delay with a timer later, but for verification the busy loop is acceptable. Repeat the pattern and observe whether any LED flickers unexpectedly — if so, check for accidental full assignments to GPIODATA that may be overwriting other bits.

keyIdea.title: Lab goal
keyIdea.text: Configure PF1–PF3 as outputs and implement a timed pattern, verifying voltages for HIGH and LOW states.

content.html:
Module 4 › Chapter 4.1 › Hands-on: Multi-LED Pattern on Port F
Activity steps
  1. Enable clock: SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO_R |= 0x20; wait for bit set.
  2. Set direction bits: GPIO_PORTF_DIR_R |= (1<<1)|(1<<2)|(1<<3);
  3. Enable digital: GPIO_PORTF_DEN_R |= (1<<1)|(1<<2)|(1<<3);
  4. In loop: set PF1, delay; clear PF1; set PF2, delay; clear PF2; set PF3, delay; clear PF3; set PF1|PF2|PF3, delay.
Use OR/AND masks to preserve other bits. After running, measure voltages on each pin when HIGH and LOW to verify electrical behavior.
Safety note
Use low-current LEDs or current-limiting resistors provided on the LaunchPad. Measure voltages, not currents, unless you know the circuit.

narration.text: These are the most important ideas to retain. First, always enable the port clock via SYSCTL_RCGCGPIO before accessing port registers. Second, use GPIODIR to select inputs or outputs and GPIODEN to enable the pin's digital function; both are required for reliable input and output. Third, perform read-modify-write with OR and AND when changing GPIODATA to avoid unintentional changes to other pins. These three concepts form the basic working pattern for GPIO on the TM4C123G and will prevent the most common faults you encounter during bring-up. As you move to more complex tasks, keep these rules front of mind and verify them early when debugging. narration.text: Keep these practical tips handy when you work on GPIO. First, always verify the clock bit reads back as set; a write alone is not enough to prove stability. Second, measure pin voltages after toggling pins to confirm electrical behavior; seeing VCC or ground on the multimeter is a quick validation. Third, reserve AFSEL pins deliberately: if you plan to use UART or PWM, configure AFSEL instead of leaving them as GPIO. These small checks will save time when the hardware does not behave as expected. Finally, use the lab checklist: enable clock, wait, set direction, enable digital, test data reads/writes, measure voltages.
